name: James K. Polk
role: 11th President of the United States (1845-1849); Speaker of the House (1835-1839)
summary: Polk was a Jacksonian Democrat who opposed national banks, protective tariffs and federal internal improvements, defended slaveholders' rights and the Union against nullification, and made territorial expansion his policy by settling Oregon and fighting Mexico for California and New Mexico.

booksNotUsed.reason: Read for the statement bank lines: the four annual messages duplicate the State of the Union texts cited from Gutenberg 5019, and the rest are procedural or transmittal messages (Oregon convention and territory, Cherokee and Mexico treaty submissions, army size and war funding, the French Republic, war-time measures). They state no position on a bank statement beyond what his inaugural, annual messages and the cited record already show.

decide-locally.rationale: He vetoed the 1846 river and harbor bill because its many local works would consolidate power in the federal government at the expense of the States and spend the common treasury on benefits to a few places, so such works were for the States.

free-trade.rationale: He signed the Walker Tariff of 1846 moving rates down to revenue-only levels and replacing ad valorem duties, according to the Miller Center.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: He asked Robert Walker to study tariff levels, then signed the Walker Tariff of 1846, which lowered rates toward revenue-only levels, according to the Miller Center.

state-directs-investment.rationale: He vetoed the bill funding internal improvements in August 1846 and had opposed federal internal improvements throughout his career.

democracy-best.rationale: He called the French people's rising a sublime spectacle and the great truth that in this enlightened age man is capable of governing himself, and said he enjoyed three-fourths of a century of well regulated self-government.

right-to-secede.rationale: He took a militant posture against South Carolina in the nullification crisis as Jackson's strongest House supporter, according to the Miller Center.

separate-church-state.rationale: He said that no union exists between church and state and that perfect freedom of opinion is guaranteed to all sects and creeds.

territorial-expansion.rationale: He secured Oregon south of 49 degrees, moved troops to the disputed Rio Grande, fought the war with Mexico and took California and New Mexico by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, according to the Miller Center.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: He voted against studying gradual abolition of slavery in the District of Columbia in 1829, voted to table anti-slavery memorials in 1833, and as president backed extending the 36°30' line to allow slavery in the southern territories, according to Voteview and the Miller Center.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: He moved troops into the disputed territory north of the Rio Grande before Mexican troops crossed the river and asked Congress for war, according to the Miller Center.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: He said all distinctions of birth or of rank have been abolished in the United States and that all citizens are placed on terms of precise equality.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: He said one great object of the Constitution was to restrain majorities from oppressing minorities and that minorities may appeal to the Constitution as a shield.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: He sent troops into disputed territory, sought to buy California through an envoy, and prosecuted the war to take Mexican territory, according to the Miller Center.

arms-reduction.rationale: He called it the settled policy to maintain in peace as small a Regular Army as the public service permits, and said the old fifteen-regiment Army would suffice in peace.

homestead-ownership.rationale: He recommended graduating and reducing public land prices for settlers and cultivators and continuing preemption in its most liberal extent for those who settle on the public lands.

no-business-privileges.rationale: He said any policy favouring monopolies or the peculiar interests of sections or classes operates to the prejudice of fellow citizens and should be avoided, and opposed institutions that make the government the instrument of classes and individuals.

money-backed-by-precious-metals.rationale: His Independent Treasury of 1846 required government disbursements in specie or in paper backed by gold or silver, according to the Miller Center.

pay-off-national-debt.rationale: He called a national debt a prop of European monarchies that transfers the labour of the many to the few, and said the debt of the last years may be speedily paid off by applying revenues not otherwise required.

remove-indigenous-peoples.rationale: As a congressman he voted in 1826 for aid to remove Creek and Florida Indians west of the Mississippi, according to Voteview. His diary records that as president he agreed to remove the New York Indians who wished to emigrate.

no-central-bank.rationale: He championed Jackson's fight against the Second Bank, voted in 1834 that the Bank of the United States not be rechartered, and as president created the Independent Treasury to replace it, according to the Miller Center and Voteview.

member-state-blocks-federal-overreach.rationale: He took a militant posture against South Carolina in the nullification crisis, according to the Miller Center.

conquest-no-lawful-claim.rationale: He took California and New Mexico by war and a treaty paying fifteen million dollars after occupying Mexico City, according to the Miller Center.

notes: First audit. Texts: his 1845 inaugural address and annual messages (Miller Center corpus, Gutenberg 5019 for the State of the Union addresses, local library), the veto of 1846; record from the Miller Center's essays by John C. Pinheiro and from Voteview roll calls of his House votes (1825-1839; as Speaker from 1835 he mostly did not vote). The uncertainty rule is not met: only 15 positions reach the lines, almost all on the economy, war and slavery; the sources hold nothing on most others. The 1846 veto answers decide-locally only on its states-versus-federal argument (a mild +1). His diary (four volumes) was searched by theme for women, religion, immigrants, taxes and local rule and holds nothing on the lines 9 and 14 statements. Not yet searched: the 1846 Cherokee messages and the 1849 war-time and treaty messages by theme, and his votes on the Force Bill and public lands.
